DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean the man whose seed begat the child. The KJV's own words for this are "begat" and "seed". I hold that the text names the Holy Ghost as the source of the conception and Mary as the only human parent in the flesh. Joseph was her husband and the child's legal father, and he was not the one who begat him.

## 1. Matthew's genealogy breaks its own pattern at Joseph

[L1] Matthew 1:2-15 repeats one formula: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob…". The formula ends at Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

[L2] The verb is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") in each earlier link. In verse 16 the verb changes to the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born/begotten"). The relative pronoun is ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), and ἧς is feminine singular. It can only refer to Mary and cannot refer to Joseph. Joseph is called ἀνήρ (anēr, "husband/man"), not the one who begat.

[L3] The same wording recurs in Matthew 1:5-6, where "of Rachab" and "of her that had been the wife of Urias" name mothers. There the father is named too, as "Salmon begat Booz of Rachab". Verse 16 withholds exactly that clause. The pattern runs "A begat B", and here it does not.

## 2. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost and not to a man

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:25: Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

[L2] In Matthew 1:20, τὸ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν (to en autē gennēthen, "that which is begotten in her") is ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου (ek pneumatos estin hagiou, "out of the Holy Ghost it is"). Here γεννάω (gennaō, "to beget") is the word for begetting, and its source is named as the Holy Ghost. In Luke 1:34, γινώσκω (ginōskō, "to know") is used of sexual relations, as in Matthew 1:25 with ἐγίνωσκεν (eginōsken, "was knowing"). Mary says she knows no ἄνδρα (andra, "man, adult male"). In Luke 1:35, ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "shall come upon") and ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "shall overshadow") describe the divine agent's action.

[L3] Luke 1:35 gives the reason for the title: "therefore also … shall be called the Son of God". Hebrews 10:5 says of the same one, "a body hast thou prepared me." The body is prepared by God and is not described as begotten by a man.

## 3. Scripture foretold a conception without a man

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." Matthew 1:22-23 says "all this was done, that it might be fulfilled." Genesis 3:15 speaks of the woman's seed. Jeremiah 31:22 says "The LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man." Galatians 4:4 says "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."

[L2] In Isaiah 7:14, עַלְמָה (almah, "young woman of marriageable age") is the word used. Matthew 1:23 renders it with παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"), and that is the KJV's word. In Genesis 24:43 almah is used of Rebekah, and Genesis 24:16 describes her as בְּתוּלָה (bethulah, "virgin"), "neither had any man known her". So almah can denote a virgin in the text. In Genesis 3:15, זַרְעָהּ (zar'ah, "her seed") is striking, because seed is ordinarily reckoned from the man. In Galatians 4:4, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman") names only the woman.

[L3] Matthew applies the Isaiah word to this very conception, and the apostle's phrase in Galatians 4:4 agrees with it. The chain runs from Genesis 3:15 through Isaiah 7:14 and Jeremiah 31:22 to Matthew 1:23 and Galatians 4:4.

## 4. "Father" language for Joseph is legal and reported opinion

[L1] Luke 3:23 says Jesus "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph". John 6:42 reports the crowd: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Luke 2:48 has Mary saying "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Luke 2:49 gives the answer: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

[L2] In Luke 3:23, ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was reckoned/supposed") marks a belief held, not a fact stated by the narrator. The verb νομίζω (nomizō, "to suppose, to hold by custom") appears also in Acts 14:19 and Acts 16:27, where the thing supposed was mistaken or uncertain.

[L3] The Luke 2:49 correction sits in the same passage as Luke 2:48. The child redirects "father" from Joseph to God. Matthew 1:19-20 shows Joseph himself was "minded to put her away privily", which means he knew the child was not his. In Matthew 1:20 the angel tells him to take Mary as "thy wife", so the legal relationship is a matter of taking her and receiving the child. It is not a matter of having begotten him.

## 5. A begotten line through Joseph would run into the bar on Coniah's seed

[L1] Jeremiah 22:30 says of Coniah, "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah." Matthew 1:11-12 places "Jechonias" in Joseph's line, and Matthew 1:16 ends that line at "Joseph the husband of Mary". Luke 1:32 promises the child "the throne of his father David". Romans 1:3 says "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

[L2] In Jeremiah 22:30, זֶרַע (zera', "seed") is the word. Elsewhere in Scripture it carries the sense of physical descent.

[L4] The text gives two footings for this inference. First, the bar in Jeremiah 22:30 applies to Coniah's seed, and Matthew 1:11-16 lists Jechonias within Joseph's line. Second, Luke 1:32 and Romans 1:3 promise the throne and the Davidic seed to the child. If Joseph had begotten Jesus, the child would be Coniah's seed and so barred from the throne. Joseph's legal fatherhood passes the claim to the throne, but the seed does not pass through his line. This is a supporting inference and not the foundation of the case.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" formula of Matthew 1:2-15 by using the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born/begotten") with the feminine ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), so Joseph is the husband of Mary and not the one who begat; footing: [L1] Matthew 1:2-16, [L2] the feminine pronoun and passive verb, [L3] the contrast with the "begat … of Rachab" pattern in Matthew 1:5.
2. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost and not to a man; footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18, 20, 25 and Luke 1:34-35, [L2] γεννηθὲν ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou, "begotten out of the Holy Ghost") and ἄνδρα/ἐγίνωσκεν (andra/eginōsken, "man"/"was knowing"), [L3] Hebrews 10:5, "a body hast thou prepared me."
3. Scripture foretold a conception without a man and the New Testament records its fulfilment; footing: [L1] Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:22-23, [L2] almah (young woman of marriageable age) rendered by parthenos (virgin), with Genesis 24:16, 43 showing almah can describe a virgin, [L3] Genesis 3:15, Jeremiah 31:22 and Galatians 4:4 ("made of a woman").
4. The texts that call Joseph "father" are reported opinion or legal relation and not begetting; footing: [L1] Luke 3:23, John 6:42, Luke 2:48-49, [L2] ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed"), [L3] Matthew 1:19-20, where Joseph himself is told to take Mary as wife.
5. A begotten line through Joseph would put Jesus under the bar on Coniah's seed, so the Davidic claim runs through legal fatherhood and not through begetting; footing: [L1] Jeremiah 22:30 with Matthew 1:11-16 and Luke 1:32, [L2] zera' (seed) in Jeremiah 22:30, [L4] the chain from the bar on Coniah's seed to Joseph's line.
6. Christ had no biological father; the Holy Ghost is named as the source of the conception, Mary is the only human parent in the flesh, and Joseph is the husband of Mary and the child's legal father; footing: links 1-5, resting on [L1] Matthew 1:16, 18, 20, 25 and Luke 1:34-35, [L2] egennēthē, gennēthen, and almah/parthenos, [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23, and Galatians 4:4.

# Defender, Round 2: Link Round, with the chain re-seated

I answer at the chain level. The challenger's rows A to F are the same four points pressed from different sides: 1) seed, loins and bowels language; 2) "father" language for Joseph; 3) the claim that "of the Holy Ghost" is only covenant origin; 4) the claim that Isaiah, Genesis and Galatians say "a mother" and never "no man". I take each point inside its chain and then give the link verdicts.

## I. Seed, loins and bowels (A against D6) is ancestral language, so it does not name an immediate begetter

[L1] The rows pressed were Romans 1:3 ("made of the seed of David according to the flesh"), Acts 2:30 ("of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh"), 2 Samuel 7:12 ("which shall proceed out of thy bowels"), Psalm 132:11 ("Of the fruit of thy body") and Hebrews 7:14 ("our Lord sprang out of Juda").

[L1] Hebrews 7:10 uses the same loins-word for remote descent: Levi "was yet in the loins of his father" Abraham, and Abraham was Levi's great-grandfather. The challenger cited Hebrews 7:5, 10 himself.

[L2] ὀσφύς (osphys, "loins") and σπέρμα (sperma, "seed, offspring") therefore reach down many generations. Romans 9:7 uses sperma the same way: "Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children."

[L3] David lived about a thousand years before this child, so "fruit of his loins" cannot name the immediate father. It names descent from David, "according to the flesh" (κατὰ σάρκα, kata sarka, "according to flesh"), meaning in bodily descent.

[L4] Footing one: Romans 1:3 requires bodily descent from David. Footing two: Matthew 1:16 uses the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born") with ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom", feminine), and Galatians 4:4 uses γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman"). If the flesh came out of the woman only, then the bodily descent from David reaches the child through her. The challenger's rows therefore do not exclude my answer. They require that the descent run through the one named as the source of the flesh.

## II. "Father" language for Joseph is reported speech or legal reckoning

[L1] The speakers are the crowd and others, not the narrator:
- Luke 4:22: "Is not this Joseph's son?"
- John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?"
- John 1:45: Philip speaks.
- Matthew 13:55 asks, "Is not this the carpenter's son?"
- Mark 6:3 has the same people say "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The same crowd names the mother, not the father.

[L1] Where the narrator speaks, he is careful. Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled." Luke 2:43: "Joseph and his mother knew not of it." In both places he says "Joseph" and does not say "his father". Luke 3:23 says "as was supposed".

[L2] The challenger set ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed") beside Acts 16:13, "was wont to be made". That helps me. νομίζω (nomizō, "to hold by custom or law") comes from νόμος (nomos, "law, custom"). At Acts 16:13 it means "was customary". At Luke 3:23 it therefore means reckoned by custom, which is legal standing and not a verdict on begetting.

[L1] The challenger's argument from naming fails. Matthew 1:21 says to Joseph "thou shalt call his name JESUS". Luke 1:31 says to Mary "thou shalt call his name JESUS". Luke 1:60 has Elisabeth naming John: "his mother answered and said, Not so; but he shall be called John."

[L1] The challenger's argument from Matthew 1:20 also fails. "Joseph, thou son of David" names Joseph's own descent. It says nothing about the child's.

[L1] Luke 1:32, "the throne of his father David", is the ancestor sense of "father". See Luke 1:73, "our father Abraham", and Luke 1:32 reads the same way for David.

[L1] Luke 2:48 has Mary saying "thy father and I", and Luke 2:49 answers "my Father's business". The correction sits in the same exchange.

## III. "Of the Holy Ghost" is tied to a conception, and the text asks and answers the question of a man

[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The reply in Luke 1:35 is "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee… therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

[L2] In Luke 1:35, διό καί (dio kai, "therefore also") makes the title follow from the way the child is conceived. The title is not a covenant label attached to an ordinary birth. The challenger's examples (2 Samuel 7:14, 1 Chronicles 28:6 about Solomon, John 1:13 "born of God") have no "therefore" tying the title to the mode of conception.

[L1] John 1:13 itself says those born of God were born "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God". Even the verse the challenger cites sets "of God" against the will of man. It is also spoken of a new birth, not of "that which is conceived in her" (Matthew 1:20).

[L2] γεννηθέν (gennēthen, "begotten") in Matthew 1:20 is the same verb as in the genealogy. The challenger says the qualifier "according to the flesh" is absent from Matthew 1:20, but it does not need to be there. The verse names the thing "conceived in her", which is already flesh in the womb.

[L2] ἐπέρχομαι (eperchomai, "come upon") and ἐπισκιάζω (episkiazō, "overshadow") can be used of empowerment, as the challenger says. At Luke 1:35 they are the answer to a question about a man, and they stand where the man would stand. That makes the context the proof, not the word taken alone.

[L3] Hebrews 10:5, "a body hast thou prepared me", and Matthew 1:18, "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost", agree. The conception is dated before they came together. Psalm 139:13 does name the maker of every man, but those texts do not also say "before they came together".

## IV. Foretelling (E against D3)

[L1] Isaiah 7:14 says "the LORD himself shall give you a sign", after the offer in Isaiah 7:11 to "ask it either in the depth, or in the height above". A sign of that order is not an ordinary conception by a husband.

[L1] The challenger moves to Isaiah 8:3-4. That child is named "Mahershalalhashbaz" (Isaiah 8:3), not Immanuel. The two are different children.

[L2] The KJV renders almah (young woman of marriageable age) as "virgin" at Isaiah 7:14. Matthew 1:23 applies the verse and uses παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"). Genesis 24:16 shows that a young woman can be described as a virgin "neither had any man known her".

[L1] Jeremiah 31:22: "The LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man." [L2] גֶּבֶר (geber, "strong man") is the man, and the verse sets the woman around him. A new thing is not the ordinary order of begetting.

[L3] I grant that Genesis 3:15, Jeremiah 31:22 and Galatians 4:4 do not each say "without a man" on their own. They are links in a chain whose stating verses are Luke 1:34-35 and Matthew 1:18-20, 25. Isaiah 28:10 is the rule of this debate: the challenger must break the chain, not one link.

## LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: SUPPORTED.** Premise: "so Joseph is the husband of Mary and not the one who begat" (D1).
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." Matthew 1:2-15 has "begat" every time.
- [L2] The verb changes from ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") to ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born") and the relative becomes feminine, ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"). Joseph is ἀνήρ (anēr, "husband"), not the begetter.
- [L3] Matthew 1:5: "Salmon begat Booz of Rachab". The mother is named there together with the father who begat. Verse 16 names only the mother in that place.
- Chain: a broken pattern, a feminine pronoun and the passive verb together state that the begetting is not ascribed to Joseph. This is not a denial read out of silence. It is the change of the verb, set beside Matthew 1:18-20. The challenger said "the sentence does not make" the denial. In Matthew 1:2-15 each husband is a begetter, and at 1:16 that is the one place it is not said.

**LINK 2: SUPPORTED.** Premise: "which means he knew the child was not his" (section 4 of the opening).
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost". Matthew 1:25: Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth".
- [L1] Matthew 1:19-20: Joseph "was minded to put her away privily." The angel's answer is "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] γάρ (gar, "for") gives the reason for the command. If Joseph had begotten the child, the reason "of the Holy Ghost" would answer a fear he did not have. ἐμνηστευθείσης (mnēsteutheisēs, "betrothed") in 1:18 puts "came together" after the betrothal, so he knew he had not yet come together with her.
- [L3] Deuteronomy 22:23-24 treats the betrothed as "his neighbour's wife" and defines the wrong as another man's act. Joseph's "just man" mind in 1:19 fits that law: a husband puts away a wife found with child by another.
- Chain: the verb of knowledge the challenger says is missing is in Matthew 1:25, "knew her not", dated before the birth. Genesis 4:1 gives the means: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 deny that knowing before the conception. The challenger's own text bounds the abstinence ("till") through the birth, so Genesis 4:1 cannot supply a begetter here.

**LINK 3: SUPPORTED.** Premise: "Scripture foretold a conception without a man and the New Testament records its fulfilment" (D3).
- [L1] Isaiah 7:14, "a virgin shall conceive", with Matthew 1:22-23, "all this was done, that it might be fulfilled".
- [L2] almah with parthenos, and Genesis 24:16, 43.
- [L3] Jeremiah 31:22 (geber, a "new thing"), Genesis 3:15 ("her seed"), Galatians 4:4 ("come to be out of a woman"), all landing on Luke 1:34-35.
- Chain: the sign of Isaiah 7:11, 14 is extraordinary, and Matthew 1:23 puts the verse on the child of Luke 1:34, where Mary says "I know not a man". The challenger's alternative, Isaiah 8:3, is a different child.

**LINK 4: SUPPORTED, as a supporting link and not the foundation.** Premise: "If Joseph had begat Jesus, the child would be Coniah's seed and so barred from the throne" (D5).
- [L1] Jeremiah 22:30: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah." Matthew 1:11-12: "Josias begat Jechonias… Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel."
- [L2] זֶרַע (zera', "seed") is begetting-language, the same word as Genesis 3:15.
- Reply to Haggai 2:23: Zerubbabel is "governor of Judah" (Haggai 1:1), not one sitting on David's throne and ruling. The signet in Haggai 2:23 is a promise, not an enthronement. Jeremiah 18:7-8 is conditional on a nation turning, and the oath in Jeremiah 22:24 ("As I live") records no such turning.
- Reply to "the legal route runs through Jechonias too": the bar speaks of "his seed", and a legal heir received by taking is not seed. Joseph's legal standing carries the right. Joseph's begetting would carry the seed. Matthew 1:16 gives Jechonias's line to Joseph and Matthew 1:18-20 withholds the begetting from him.
- Reply to Luke 3:27: Luke never uses "begat". He uses the genitive "of", and Luke 3:23 has Joseph "the son of Heli" while Matthew 1:16 has "Jacob begat Joseph". Two fathers for one man show that "son of" in Luke is not always begetting. Ezra 2:61 shows a man called by his wife's father's name, and Numbers 27:1-7 and 36:6-8 show inheritance passing through daughters.

**LINK 5: SUPPORTED.** Premise: "Mary is the only human parent in the flesh" (D6).
- [L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh". Matthew 1:16 ("of whom", feminine), Luke 1:31 ("thou shalt conceive in thy womb"), Luke 1:42 ("the fruit of thy womb"), Galatians 4:4.
- [L2] σάρξ (sarx, "flesh") in Romans 1:3 requires bodily descent from David. ἐξ ἧς and ἐκ γυναικός name the woman alone as the source of the flesh.
- [L3] Numbers 1:2 and 1:18 are the census of the males mustered by fathers' houses, and Numbers 36:6-8 shows inheritance passing through daughters. The challenger's own reading of Luke 1:27 and 2:4 fixes Joseph's house but names no house for Mary either way. Silence about her house does not deny her descent.
- [L4] Footing one: Romans 1:3 requires bodily descent from David. Footing two: Matthew 1:16 and Galatians 4:4 name the woman as the sole source of the flesh. If both hold, Mary's flesh carries the descent. That is why the descent is "according to the flesh" and not "according to the house".

Everything the challenger raised in sections A to F and did not answer stands as held for me. In particular: the ancestral sense of loins, "his father David", the same crowd naming Mary alone in Mark 6:3, Luke 1:60, dio kai in Luke 1:35, and the date "before they came together" in Matthew 1:18.

# CHALLENGER — ROUND 1

**Opening.** The question is narrow: was there a man whose seed begat the child? The defender says no. I answer that the text names the father in four registers, requires the promised seed out of a man's own body "according to the flesh," and states the canon's means of begetting. "Of the Holy Ghost" is the covenant-origin marker, not a begetter. I aim at the keystone **D6** and at **D2**, **D1**, **D3**, **D4**, **D5** beneath it.

---

## A. TARGET LINK D6 (and D2) — the seed rows state a man's body; "no biological father" is the contrary of what is written

[L1] Romans 1:3 — "Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, **which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh**."

[L1] Acts 2:30 — "of the **fruit of his loins, according to the flesh**, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."

[L1] 2 Samuel 7:12 — "I will set up thy seed after thee, **which shall proceed out of thy bowels**." [L1] Psalm 132:11 — "**Of the fruit of thy body** will I set upon thy throne." [L1] Hebrews 7:14 — "it is **evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda**."

[L2] The anatomy of those rows: 2 Samuel 7:12 is mimme'eykha (out of thy bowels); Acts 2:30 is osphys (loins), the same loins-word of Hebrews 7:5, 10; Romans 1:3 is ek spermatos Dauid kata sarka (out of the seed of David, according to flesh) — seed and flesh, a begetting, not a legal transfer.

[L3] The reckoning rows fix what "evident" means: Numbers 1:2 "by the house of their fathers ... every male by their polls"; 1:18 "declared their pedigrees ... by the house of their fathers." The line is counted down the father.

**D6 states the contrary of these verses.** It says there was no man who begat; these say seed proceeding out of a man's bowels, fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, and that the descent is evident. A defence that severs the seed from every man's body cannot stand beside "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh" [L1]. And the defender's route through Mary leaves Numbers 1:2 unanswered: the text names Joseph's house — "of the house of David" (Luke 1:27), "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4) — and names no house for Mary [L1]. The claim "Mary is the only human parent in the flesh" is an import the reckoning rows do not carry.

## B. TARGET LINK D2 — "of the Holy Ghost" is covenant origin; the same preposition pattern is used of men with fathers

[L1] Matthew 1:20 — "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Compare the same construction of men who had fathers: John 1:13 "born of God"; 1 John 5:1 "whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God"; 1 John 3:9 "born of God"; 1 John 4:7 "is of God." [L2] All are ek + God/Spirit, and every one is covenant or spiritual origin, never biological paternity. Where the text means flesh-begotten it marks it: Romans 1:3 kata sarka ("according to the flesh") — the qualifier is absent at Matthew 1:20.

[L1] Luke 1:35 — "The Holy Ghost shall **come upon** thee, and the power of the Highest shall **overshadow** thee." [L2] eperchomai (come upon) is the empowerment word of Acts 1:8 "after that the Holy Ghost is **come upon** you, and ye shall be witnesses unto me"; episkiazō (overshadow) is the presence-cloud word at Matthew 17:5, Mark 9:7, Luke 9:34 (the transfiguration cloud) and Acts 5:15 (Peter's shadow). Neither denotes begetting at any row.

[L1] The title in that verse is a covenant title given to a man with a father: 2 Samuel 7:14 "I will be his father, and he shall be my son"; 1 Chronicles 28:6 "Solomon thy son ... I have chosen him to be my son" — Solomon, David's own son; Psalm 2:7 "this day have I begotten thee," applied at Acts 13:33 to the resurrection, and Luke 1:35 says the child "shall be **called** the Son of God." [L3] So "of the Holy Ghost" plus "Son of God" never states divine paternity of flesh.

[L1] The defender's [L3] Hebrews 10:5 "a body hast thou prepared me" names the maker of the body. [L3] Psalm 139:13 "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb" is said of every man. Naming the maker excludes no father.

**D2 is answered:** the conception rows name the child's covenant origin and the mother; they do not say "no man." And [L1] John 6:42 states the contrary on the same matter: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, **whose father and mother we know**?"

## C. TARGET LINK D1 — the passive verb is non-narration, and the father is named in four registers

[L1] Matthew 1:16 "of whom was born Jesus" does not state who begat; it does not say "no man." To read "not the one who begat" out of a passive verb is to supply a denial the sentence does not make [L4]. Against it the canon speaks plainly:

- Mary: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48).
- The narrator: "the parents brought in the child Jesus" (Luke 2:27); "his parents went to Jerusalem" (2:41); "Joseph and his mother marvelled" (2:33, 43).
- The town and a disciple: "Is not this Joseph's son?" (Luke 4:22); "Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know" (John 6:42); "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45).

# SYNTHESIS — Chain-Scoped Assessment

**Method note.** Both sides were assessed by whether they engaged chains as chains or stripped isolated terms (Isaiah 28:10). The defender is a plain seat; the challenger is the seat that carries the drift guards, and only that seat is tested under them (§3). A point appears in §1 only if no charge on either side contests it; charged points are carried into §2 with both sides' answers. No round followed the challenger's link round in this format, so silence after that point is procedural and counts against neither side.

---

## 1. What held at L1–L2–L3 (uncontested)

1. **The formula change at Matthew 1:16.** Matthew 1:2–15 uses the active ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*, "begat") of each father; 1:16 shifts to the passive ἐγεννήθη (*egennēthē*, "was born") with the feminine relative ἐξ ἧς (*ex hēs*, "of whom"), and Joseph is titled ἀνήρ (*anēr*, "husband"). Neither side disputed the grammar; only the inference.
2. **Joseph is husband in law from the espousal.** "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19); "Mary thy wife" (1:20); Deuteronomy 22:24 calls the betrothed "his neighbour's wife." Both sides affirm this.
3. **Joseph performed the father's naming act.** "Thou shalt call his name JESUS" (Matthew 1:21), done at 1:25. Both cite it; only its import is disputed.
4. **Joseph's house is David's.** Matthew 1:20 "thou son of David"; Luke 1:27 "of the house of David"; Luke 2:4 "of the house and lineage of David"; Luke 1:32 "the throne of his father David."
5. **The conception is "of the Holy Ghost."** Matthew 1:18, 20; Luke 1:35 names the Spirit's coming upon (*eperchomai*) and overshadowing (*episkiazō*) as the answer to Mary's question. Undisputed at L1–L2.
6. **The canon's stated means of begetting.** "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1). Both sides cite it; they divide only on whether it can reach this conception.
7. **No knowing before the birth.** "Knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matthew 1:25). Both agree.
8. **The seed/loins rows are David-descent language.** Romans 1:3; Acts 2:30; 2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 132:11; Hebrews 7:14. Both agree they name Davidic descent "according to the flesh"; the dispute is what they require at the last link.
